paragraphs: Mitya could hardly catch his breath as he poured out this wild speech. He had gone pale, his lips trembled, and tears were running down his cheeks.

“Yes, life is full. There is life even underground,” he began again. “You won’t believe it, Alexey, but I want to live so badly now. Within these peeling walls a thirst for existence and awareness has sprung up in me. Rakitin doesn’t understand that. All he cares about is building a house and renting out apartments. But I’ve been longing for you. And what is suffering? I’m not afraid of it, even if there were no counting it. I’m not afraid of it now. I was afraid of it before. Do you know, maybe I won’t answer at the trial at all.... And I seem to have such strength in me now that I think I could stand anything, any suffering, if only I can say and keep saying to myself every moment, ‘I exist.’ In a thousand agonies—I exist. Tormented on the rack—I exist! Even if I sit alone on a pillar—I exist! I see the sun, and if I don’t see the sun, I know it’s there. And there’s a whole life in that, in knowing the sun is there. Alyosha, my angel, all these philosophies are killing me. Damn them! Brother Ivan—”
“What about brother Ivan?” Alyosha cut in, but Mitya didn’t hear.

“You see, I never had any of these doubts before, but it was all hidden away in me. Maybe it was just because ideas I didn’t understand were surging up in me that I used to drink and brawl and rage. I wanted to choke them in myself, to quiet them, to smother them. Ivan is not Rakitin. There is an idea in him. Ivan is a sphinx, and he is silent. He is always silent. It’s God that’s worrying me. That’s the only thing that worries me. What if He doesn’t exist? What if Rakitin is right, and it’s just an idea made up by men? Then, if He doesn’t exist, man is the master of the earth, of the whole universe. Magnificent! Only how is he going to be good without God? That’s the question. I always come back to it. Whom is man going to love then? Who will he be thankful to? Who will he sing the hymn to? Rakitin laughs. Rakitin says you can love humanity without God. Well, only a sniveling idiot can claim that. I can’t understand it. Life’s easy for Rakitin. ‘You’d do better to think about extending civil rights, or even about keeping down the price of meat. You’ll show your love for humanity more simply and directly that way than with philosophy.’ And I answered him, ‘Well, but you, without a God, are more likely to raise the price of meat, if it suits you, and make a rouble on every kopeck.’ He lost his temper. But after all, what is goodness? Answer me that, Alexey. Goodness is one thing for me and another for a Chinese man, so it’s relative. Or isn’t it? Isn’t it relative? A treacherous question! You won’t laugh if I tell you it’s kept me awake two nights. I only wonder now how people can live and never think about it. Vanity! Ivan has no God. He has an idea. It’s beyond me. But he is silent. I think he’s a Freemason. I asked him, but he is silent. I wanted to drink from the springs of his soul—he was silent. But once he did let a word drop.”
“What did he say?” Alyosha asked quickly.

“I said to him, ‘Then everything is lawful, if that’s how it is?’ He frowned. ‘Fyodor Pavlovitch, our papa,’ he said, ‘was a pig, but his ideas were right enough.’ That was what he let drop. That was all he said. That goes one better than Rakitin.”
“Yes,” Alyosha agreed bitterly. “When was he with you?”

“I’ll tell you that later. Now I have to talk about something else. I haven’t said anything about Ivan to you before. I put it off till the last. When my business here is over and the verdict has been given, then I’ll tell you something. I’ll tell you everything. We have something tremendous on hand.... And you shall be my judge in it. But don’t start on that now. Be quiet. You talk about tomorrow, about the trial, but, would you believe it, I know nothing about it.”
“Have you talked to your lawyer?”

“What’s the use of the lawyer? I told him all about it. He’s a soft, city-bred rogue—a Bernard! But he doesn’t believe me—not a bit of it. Just imagine, he believes I did it. I can see it. ‘In that case,’ I asked him, ‘why have you come to defend me?’ Hang them all! They’ve brought a doctor down too, to prove I’m mad. I won’t have that! Katerina Ivanovna wants to do her ‘duty’ to the end, whatever the strain!” Mitya smiled bitterly. “The cat! Hard-hearted creature! She knows I said of her at Mokroe that she was a woman of ‘great wrath.’ They repeated it. Yes, the facts against me have grown as numerous as the sands of the sea. Grigory sticks to his story. Grigory’s honest, but a fool. Plenty of people are honest because they’re fools: that’s Rakitin’s idea. Grigory’s my enemy. And some people are better as enemies than as friends. I mean Katerina Ivanovna. I’m afraid, oh, I’m afraid she’ll tell how she bowed to the ground after that four thousand. She’ll pay it back to the last penny. I don’t want her sacrifice. They’ll put me to shame at the trial. I wonder how I can stand it. Go to her, Alyosha, and ask her not to speak of that in court. Can you do that? But damn it all, it doesn’t matter! I’ll get through somehow. I don’t pity her. It’s her own doing. She deserves what she gets. I’ll have my own story to tell, Alexey.” He smiled bitterly again. “Only ... only Grusha, Grusha! Good Lord! Why should she have such suffering to bear?” he suddenly cried, with tears. “Grusha’s killing me. The thought of her is killing me, killing me. She was with me just now....”
“She told me you hurt her very much today.”
“I know. Curse my temper! It was jealousy. I was sorry. I kissed her as she was leaving. I didn’t ask her forgiveness.”
“Why not?” Alyosha exclaimed.
Suddenly Mitya laughed, almost merrily.

“God keep you, my dear boy, from ever asking forgiveness for a fault from a woman you love. Especially from one you love, however much in the wrong you may have been. Because a woman—the devil only knows what to make of a woman! I know something about them, anyway. But just try admitting you’re in the wrong to a woman. Say, ‘I’m sorry, forgive me,’ and a shower of reproaches will follow! She’ll never simply and directly forgive you. She’ll grind you into the dust, drag in things that never happened, recall everything, forget nothing, add something of her own, and only then forgive you. And even the best of them, the very best, do it. She’ll scrape up all the scrapings and load them on your head. They’re ready to flay you alive, I tell you, every one of them, all these angels we can’t live without! I tell you plainly and openly, dear boy, every decent man ought to be under some woman’s thumb. That’s my conviction—not conviction, but feeling. A man ought to be magnanimous, and it’s no disgrace to him! No disgrace to a hero, not even to a Cæsar! But all the same, never beg her pardon for anything. Remember that rule from your brother Mitya, who has been ruined by women. No, I’d better make it up to Grusha somehow, without begging pardon. I worship her, Alexey, worship her. Only she doesn’t see it. No, she still thinks I don’t love her enough. And she tortures me, tortures me with her love. The past was nothing! In the past it was only those infernal curves of hers that tortured me, but now I’ve taken her whole soul into my soul, and through her I’ve become a man myself. Will they let us marry? If they don’t, I’ll die of jealousy. I imagine something every day.... What did she say to you about me?”
Alyosha repeated everything Grushenka had said to him that day. Mitya listened, made him repeat certain things, and seemed pleased.

“Then she isn’t angry at my being jealous?” he exclaimed. “What a woman she is! ‘I’ve a fierce heart myself!’ Ah, I love such fierce hearts, though I can’t bear anyone being jealous of me. I can’t stand it. We’ll fight. But I’ll love her, I’ll love her endlessly. Will they let us marry? Do they let convicts marry? That’s the question. And without her I can’t exist....”
Mitya paced across the room, frowning. It was almost dark. He suddenly seemed terribly worried.

“So there’s a secret, she says, a secret? We’ve cooked up a plot against her, and Katya is mixed up in it, she thinks. No, my good Grushenka, that’s not it. You’re very wide of the mark, in your foolish woman’s way. Alyosha, darling, well, here goes! I’ll tell you our secret!”

He looked around, went quickly up to Alyosha, who was standing in front of him, and whispered to him with an air of mystery, though in fact no one could hear them. The old warder was dozing in the corner, and not a word could reach the ears of the soldiers on guard.

“I’ll tell you our whole secret,” Mitya whispered hurriedly. “I meant to tell you later, because how could I decide anything without you? You are everything to me. Though I say Ivan is superior to us, you are my angel. It’s your decision that will decide it. Maybe it’s you who are superior, and not Ivan. You see, it’s a question of conscience, a question of the higher conscience—the secret is so important that I can’t settle it myself, and I’ve put it off till I could speak to you. But anyway it’s too early to decide now, because we have to wait for the verdict. As soon as the verdict is given, you shall decide my fate. Don’t decide it now. I’ll tell you now. You listen, but don’t decide. Stand there and keep quiet. I won’t tell you everything. I’ll only tell you the idea, without details, and you keep quiet. Not a question, not a movement. Agreed? But, good heavens, what am I going to do about your eyes? I’m afraid your eyes will tell me your decision, even if you don’t speak. Oh! I’m afraid! Alyosha, listen! Ivan suggests that I _escape_. I won’t tell you the details: it’s all been thought out, it can all be arranged. Hush, don’t decide. I would go to America with Grusha. You know I can’t live without Grusha! What if they won’t let her follow me to Siberia? Do they let convicts get married? Ivan thinks not. And without Grusha what would I do there underground with a hammer? I’d only smash my skull with the hammer! But then, on the other hand, my conscience? I would have run away from suffering. A sign has come, and I reject the sign. I have a way of salvation, and I turn my back on it. Ivan says that in America, ‘with the good will,’ I can be of more use than underground. But what becomes of our hymn from underground? What is America? America is vanity again! And there’s a lot of swindling in America too, I expect. I would have run away from crucifixion! I’m telling you, Alexey, because you are the only person who can understand this. There’s no one else. To others it’s folly, madness, all I’ve told you about the hymn. They’ll say I’m out of my mind or a fool. I’m not out of my mind and I’m not a fool. Ivan understands about the hymn too. He understands, only he doesn’t answer—he doesn’t speak. He doesn’t believe in the hymn. Don’t speak, don’t speak. I see how you look! You’ve already decided. Don’t decide, spare me! I can’t live without Grusha. Wait till after the trial!”
Mitya ended beside himself. He held Alyosha by the shoulders with both hands, and his yearning, feverish eyes were fixed on his brother’s.
“They don’t let convicts marry, do they?” he repeated for the third time, in a pleading voice.
Alyosha listened with extreme surprise and was deeply moved.
“Tell me one thing,” he said. “Is Ivan very keen on it, and whose idea was it?”

“His, his, and he is very keen on it. He didn’t come to see me at first. Then he suddenly came a week ago and started on it right away. He is terribly keen on it. He doesn’t ask me, he orders me to escape. He has no doubt I’ll obey him, though I showed him all my heart as I have to you, and told him about the hymn too. He told me he’d arrange it. He’s found out about everything. But more of that later. He’s simply set on it. It’s all a matter of money: he’ll pay ten thousand for the escape and give me twenty thousand for America. And he says we can arrange a magnificent escape for ten thousand.”
“And he told you on no account to tell me?” Alyosha asked again.
“To tell no one, and especially not you. On no account to tell you. He’s afraid, no doubt, that you’ll stand in front of me as my conscience. Don’t tell him I told you. Don’t tell him, for anything.”

“You’re right,” Alyosha declared. “It’s impossible to decide anything before the trial is over. After the trial you’ll decide for yourself. Then you’ll find that new man in yourself, and he will decide.”
“A new man, or a Bernard who’ll decide _à la_ Bernard, because I think I’m a contemptible Bernard myself,” said Mitya, with a bitter grin.
“But, brother, have you no hope then of being acquitted?”

Mitya shrugged his shoulders nervously and shook his head. “Alyosha, darling, it’s time for you to go,” he said, with sudden haste. “The superintendent is shouting in the yard. He’ll be here any moment. We’re late. It’s against the rules. Embrace me quickly. Kiss me! Make the sign of the cross over me, darling, for the cross I have to bear tomorrow.”
They embraced and kissed.
“Ivan,” said Mitya suddenly, “suggests that I escape. But of course he believes I did it.”
A mournful smile came to his lips.
“Have you asked him whether he believes it?” asked Alyosha.
“No, I haven’t. I wanted to, but I couldn’t. I didn’t have the courage. But I saw it in his eyes. Well, good-by!”
Once more they kissed hurriedly, and Alyosha was just going out when Mitya suddenly called him back.

“Stand facing me! That’s right!” And again he seized Alyosha, putting both hands on his shoulders. His face suddenly went deathly pale, so that it was dreadfully plain even through the gathering darkness. His lips twitched, and his eyes were fixed on Alyosha.
“Alyosha, tell me the whole truth, as you would before God. Do you believe I did it? Do you, do you yourself, believe it? The whole truth, don’t lie!” he cried desperately.
Everything seemed to heave before Alyosha, and he felt something like a stab in his heart.
“Hush! What do you mean?” he faltered helplessly.
“The whole truth, the whole, don’t lie!” repeated Mitya.
“I’ve never for one instant believed that you were the murderer!” burst in a shaking voice from Alyosha’s breast, and he raised his right hand in the air, as though calling God to witness his words.
Mitya’s whole face lit up with bliss.

“Thank you!” he said slowly, like someone letting out a sigh after fainting. “Now you’ve given me new life. Would you believe it, till this moment I’ve been afraid to ask you, you, even you. Well, go! You’ve given me strength for tomorrow. God bless you! Come, go along! Love Ivan!” were Mitya’s last words.

Alyosha went out in tears. Such distrust in Mitya, such lack of confidence even in him, in Alyosha—all this suddenly opened before Alyosha an unsuspected depth of hopeless grief and despair in his unhappy brother’s soul. Intense, boundless compassion overwhelmed him at once. His torn heart ached sharply. “Love Ivan!”—he suddenly remembered Mitya’s words. And he was going to Ivan. He had badly wanted to see Ivan all day. He was as worried about Ivan as about Mitya, and more than ever now.
